# Comparative effectiveness of stereotactic, subdural, or hybrid intracranial EEG monitoring in epilepsy surgery

**Authors:** Rohan Jha; David D. Liu; Jakob V. E. Gerstl; Sophia Renauld; John L. Kilgallon; Sarah E. Blitz; Lila Medeiros; Noah L. A. Nawabi; Hargunbir Singh; Melissa M. J. Chua; Steven Tobochnik; G. Rees Cosgrove; John D. Rolston

**Affiliations:** 1Harvard Medical School, Boston | 2Department of Neurosurgery, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston | 3Harvard MIT MD PhD Program, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | 4Department of Neurology, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston

## Abstract

Surgical intervention can be curative or palliative for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. However, if the seizure onset zone (SOZ) cannot be adequately localized via noninvasive tests, intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings are often carried out to develop surgical plans in appropriate candidates. Stereotactic EEG (SEEG), subdural EEG (SDE), and SDE with depth electrodes (hybrid) are major tools used for investigation, but there is no class 1 or 2 evidence comparing the effectiveness of these modalities.

The authors identified an institutional cohort of patients who underwent iEEG monitoring between 2001 and 2022. Demographic data, preoperative clinical features, iEEG intervention, and follow-up data were identified. Primary study endpoints included the following: 1) likelihood of SOZ localization; 2) likelihood of surgical treatment after iEEG; 3) seizure outcomes; and 4) complications.

A total of 329 patients were identified (176 in the SEEG, 60 in the SDE, and 93 in the hybrid cohort) who were followed for a median of 5.4 (IQR 6.8) years. Baseline characteristics, including demographics, mean age at epilepsy diagnosis, mean age at iEEG investigation, number of preoperative antiseizure medications, and preoperative seizure frequency, were not statistically different across the 3 cohorts. Patients in the SEEG cohort were more likely to have their SOZ localized than were the patients in the SDE group (OR 2.3) and were less likely to undergo subsequent resection (OR 0.3) or to have complications (OR 0.4), although there was no statistical difference with respect to likelihood of undergoing any subsequent neurosurgical treatment, or with respect to favorable seizure outcomes. Patients in the hybrid cohort were more likely to have SOZ localized than were patients in the SDE group (OR 3.1), but were more likely to undergo resection (OR 4.9) or any neurosurgical treatment (OR 2.5) compared to patients in the SEEG group. Patients in the hybrid cohort had better seizure outcomes compared to the SDE (OR 2.3) but not to the SEEG group.

Patients in the SEEG group were more likely to have their SOZ localized and patients in the SDE group were more likely to undergo resection, but they did not differ with respect to seizure outcomes.

Epilepsy affects approximately 1% of the population, with pharmacoresistant epilepsy affecting 30%–35% of people with epilepsy.1,2 These patients with inadequate control of their seizures despite aggressive drug therapy are at increased risk for accidental injuries, status epilepticus, and sudden unexpected death.3 The mechanisms of drug resistance are still poorly understood, and in many cases nonpharmacological interventions lead to improved rates of seizure palliation or seizure-free status.4,5 Multiple meta-analyses and randomized prospective trials have shown that epilepsy surgery is more effective than medical therapy for seizure control.6,7

Prior to surgical intervention, patients require accurate identification and localization of the seizure onset zone (SOZ).8 Surgical candidates often first undergo extensive noninvasive presurgical evaluation, including continuous scalp electroencephalography (EEG) with video monitoring, MRI, metabolic imaging such as PET or SPECT, magnetoencephalography, and other modalities as clinically indicated to predict the SOZ.9–11 In approximately 50%–60% of cases, these noninvasive modalities may be of sufficient localizing value to proceed with curative or palliative epilepsy surgery.4

However, in the remaining cases with discordant electroclinical results or poorly localized SOZ, invasive monitoring with direct brain recording is necessary to adequately localize the SOZ.12–14 Furthermore, noninvasive tests lack spatial resolution for surgical planning; hence, in cases in which the putative SOZ is near eloquent brain regions, invasive monitoring via intracranial EEG (iEEG) serves a critical role in determining the boundaries of safe resection.15 iEEG investigations typically involve either subdural EEG (SDE) or stereotactic EEG (SEEG). SDE monitoring involves craniotomy and placement of grids and strip electrodes to record cortical activity over the surface of the brain. Alternatively, SEEG is a less invasive procedure in which depth electrodes are placed through subcentimeter burr holes traversing from superficial cortical layers to deep brain structures. SDE electrodes densely cover the superficial cortex and are considered particularly beneficial in functionally mapping eloquent cortex to create a guide for resection around these critical areas.9,16,17 Given that SDE requires a craniotomy, resection can be offered and is often preformed after monitoring during the same hospitalization. SEEG is often preferred for suspected seizure foci in deep structures, to provide bilateral or multifocal coverage, and in patients who have undergone prior craniotomies and resection.2,12,16,18,19

Historically, SEEG has primarily been used in Europe, whereas North American centers have preferred SDE.2,14,18 However, in the last decade SEEG has increasingly become the preferred modality in North American epilepsy surgery practice, such that since 2016, SEEG has become the most frequently performed intracranial monitoring procedure. Advances in neuroimaging, stereotactic targeting, and robotics have spearheaded this increasing use.20–22 Nevertheless, this shift has occurred with limited scientific data. No class 1 or class 2 evidence exists to compare the 2 iEEG practices.18 Randomized controlled trials comparing the 2 modalities are impossible, because there is a lack of equipoise at both individual surgeon and institutional levels, leading to clinical standards of care based on underlying epilepsy syndrome and patient-specific preferences.23,24 Current evidence is limited to consensus-based expert recommendation from the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) identifying the perceived strengths and weaknesses of the modalities,25 retrospective cohorts limited in sample size, restricted time periods, unequal cohort distribution, and baseline differences between patients undergoing each modality,14,26,27 and meta-analyses with significant heterogeneity and confounders between studies.28,29

We report on one of the largest single-institution retrospective cohorts of patients who underwent iEEG using SDE, SEEG, or SDE with simultaneous depth electrode placement (hybrid). We present evidence comparing the yield of the iEEG technique on the likelihood of subsequent neurosurgical intervention, achieving favorable seizure outcomes, and associated complications/morbidity. We leverage institutional practices to identify the use cases and effect of hybrid iEEG on these outcomes, which has been rarely reported on previously. Finally, although analyses in the literature have often been limited to resection, we additionally characterize the association of iEEG technique with the availability and increasing use of nonresective surgical interventions for epilepsy, including neuromodulation and laser ablation.

## Methods

### Patient Cohort

We used retrospective chart review to identify patients with epilepsy who underwent iEEG monitoring with depth electrodes and/or subdural grids/strips at Mass General Brigham between 2001 and 2022. Procedures with frame-based and robot-based depth electrodes were designated as SEEG. Procedures involving craniotomy and subdural grids and/or strip electrodes were designated as SDE. Finally, patients who underwent craniotomy with subdural grids and/or strip electrodes, which is similar to SDE but with depth electrodes sutured in, were designated as a third, distinct category (hybrid). Patients with foramen ovale electrodes were excluded. For patients who underwent multiple iEEG investigations, we only included and analyzed the outcomes from the first implantation. However, many patients had undergone prior investigations at other institutions, including pediatric hospitals, for which we did not have complete data. For patients who underwent multiple subsequent neurosurgical interventions, only outcomes from the first intervention following iEEG monitoring were analyzed.

Patient demographic information was extracted from the electronic medical health record. Preoperative clinical and epilepsy features were extracted. Features of iEEG investigation parameters, invasive monitoring–related complications, subsequent neurosurgical interventions in treatment of epilepsy, and clinical follow-up course were also recorded.

### Assessment of Outcomes

Primary outcomes that were evaluated included likelihood of subsequent neurosurgical intervention, likelihood of complication, and likelihood of favorable seizure outcomes. The SOZ was considered localized if the multidisciplinary conference or neurologist documentation identified electrographic onsets within a specific lobar or sub-lobar brain area. Surgical complications that were included for analyses included wound or intracranial infections, subdural hematomas (SDHs), radiographic intraparenchymal hemorrhage (IPH), and infarctions. Cases requiring electrode revisions and reoperations were also identified. Complication outcomes were reported both as a function of individual complications and as a summed composite. There were no deaths following iEEG, so this was not analyzed separately. Favorable seizure outcomes were assessed as the proportion of patients who achieved complete freedom from disabling seizures. In addition, seizure outcomes were also stratified by different Engel surgical outcomes, wherever possible. Seizure outcomes were determined from clinical notes at the latest outpatient follow-up.

### Statistical Methods

We used MATLAB 2023a (The MathWorks, Inc.) for all statistical analyses. Figures were generated with R version 4.3.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing). Baseline clinical characteristics were statistically compared using the 2-sided Student t-test for continuous variables, and Pearson’s chi-square test for categorial variables. Likelihood ratios for outcomes were identified with logistic regression. All data are presented as the median (IQR) unless otherwise indicated, and all significance was set at p < 0.05.

## Results

### Preoperative Clinical Characteristics and Investigation Parameters

A total of 329 unique patients underwent invasive monitoring using SEEG, SDE, or a hybrid of the 2 modalities over the course of 2 decades, with a median postoperative follow-up period of 5.4 (IQR 6.8) years. Overall, 53.5% underwent SEEG, 18.2% underwent SDE, and 28.3% underwent hybrid monitoring. The choice of procedure shifted over this time, with SEEG, SDE, and hybrid performed in 27.7%, 31.1%, and 41.2% between 2001 and 2012 (prior to FDA approval of responsive neurostimulation [RNS]), and 68.1%, 11.0%, and 21.0% performed between 2013 and 2022, respectively.

Patients in all 3 cohorts had similar baseline preoperative characteristics (Fig. 1), except for the presence of bilateral generalized tonic-clonic (GTC) seizures and having undergone preoperative PET imaging. Patients undergoing SEEG monitoring were more likely to have GTC seizures than patients monitored with either SDE or the hybrid modality (89% vs 65% vs 73%, p < 0.0001). Patients undergoing SEEG and hybrid monitoring were more likely to have a preoperative PET scan carried out than were those who underwent SDE (82% vs 78% vs 48%, p < 0.0001).

The median age at surgery was 34 (IQR 22), 31 (IQR 14), and 28 (IQR 17) years for the SEEG, SDE, and hybrid cohorts, respectively. In addition, the median duration of epilepsy was 17 (IQR 19), 14 (IQR 16), and 15 (IQR 19) years, respectively. With respect to antiseizure medications (ASMs), patients who had SEEG, SDE, and hybrid monitoring were on a median of 3 (IQR 1), 2 (IQR 1), and 3 (IQR 2) ASMs, respectively. Preoperative seizure frequency was highly variable in patients, with a median of 8 (IQR 28) seizures per month. The preoperative MRI demonstrated lesions in 66.6% of patients (Fig. 1). The presumed etiology was identified in 61.7% of patients, with posttraumatic/ischemic changes, malformation of cortical development (MCD), mesial temporal sclerosis (MTS), tumor, and encephalitis forming the majority of the likely etiologies (Fig. 1).

Patients were much more likely to have unilateral iEEG investigations with SDE or hybrid placement of grids and electrodes, when compared to SEEG (76% vs 18% vs 23%, p < 0.0001) (Fig. 2). The median length of monitoring trended higher in the SEEG and hybrid cohorts (8.0 vs 8.0 vs 7.0 days, p < 0.0001) (Fig. 2).

### SOZ Localization and Likelihood of Subsequent Treatment

The SOZ was clinically localized in 90% of patients in the SEEG, 80% in the SDE, and 92% in the hybrid cohort. This corresponded to a higher likelihood of SOZ localization in patients who underwent SEEG when compared to SDE (OR 2.3, 95% CI 1.04–5.2). Similarly, the hybrid modality compared to SDE led to better localization (OR 3.1, 95% CI 1.1–8.3). Patients who had SEEG monitoring did not differ statistically from the hybrid monitoring cohort with respect to likelihood of SOZ localization (Fig. 3, Table 1).

Subsequent neurosurgical intervention for epilepsy was performed in 81% of SEEG cases, 83% of SDE cases, and 91% of hybrid cases. This corresponded to a higher likelihood of subsequent treatment in the hybrid cohort compared to SEEG (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.1–5.7). Patients in the SDE cohort were not statistically different with respect to likelihood of subsequent neurosurgical intervention when compared to those in the SEEG or hybrid cohorts. Of the interventions for epilepsy treatment, resection was performed most often, but RNS, laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT), vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and multiple subpial transections (MST) were also carried out.

Hybrid iEEG was associated with a higher likelihood of patients undergoing resection when compared to the SEEG cohort (OR 4.9, 95% CI 2.7–9.0). Notably, patients in the SEEG group were also less likely to undergo resection than those in the SDE group (OR 0.3, 95% CI 0.2–0.5). However, after 2013, there was no statistical difference between the SEEG and SDE cohorts (p = 0.681). Similarly, there was no difference between hybrid and SEEG modalities with respect to likelihood of subsequent resection.

### Seizure Outcomes

Patients with follow-up longer than 1 year were evaluated for seizure outcomes. This included a cohort of 167 patients who underwent SEEG monitoring, 55 who underwent SDE, and 90 who received hybrid monitoring. In patients who underwent resective surgery after iEEG, 46% had favorable seizure outcomes at last follow-up after SEEG-guided resection, as opposed to 58% and 37% in SDE-guided and hybrid guided resections, respectively. Odds of seizure freedom following resection were higher (OR 2.3, 95% CI 1.1–5.0) for patients undergoing SDE as compared to hybrid monitoring, and similar to patients undergoing SEEG monitoring (OR 1.6, 95% CI 0.8–3.4) (Fig. 3, Table 2).

In patients who underwent neuromodulation following iEEG investigation, similar rates of favorable seizure outcomes were observed among the iEEG modalities.

### Surgical Complications

In the SEEG cohort, 11% of patients had any complication, compared to 23% after SDE-guided implantation or 24% after hybrid guided implantation. Details of complications by type are identified in Table 3. Patients in the SEEG cohort were statistically less likely to have complications than those in the SDE group (OR 0.4, 95% CI 0.2–0.9). Similarly, patients in the hybrid cohort were more likely to have complications than those in the SEEG group (OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.2–4.7). Patients in the SEEG group were less likely to have infections than those in the SDE cohort (OR 0.03, 95% CI 0.004–0.3). Patients in the SEEG cohort trended toward having a lower likelihood of SDHs than those in the SDE and hybrid groups. No significance or trends were observed with respect to IPH, infarcts, repositioning, and reoperations, although analyses were limited by the small number of observed specific complications in each cohort (Fig. 3, Table 3).

Favorable seizure outcome rates were not associated with the presence of any individual or pooled complications, across each iEEG modality and in aggregate. Similarly, Engel outcomes were not statistically influenced by complications. In patients who were not seizure free, there was no statistical difference in the ratio index of preoperative/postoperative seizure rate (p = 0.207) in patients with and without complications. Finally, there was no change in the number of ASMs between the preoperative and last follow-up time point in patients with and without complications.

## Discussion

iEEG is an essential tool in delineating the SOZ and mapping eloquent cortex in patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. However, the need for multiple procedures and the potential morbidity of these procedures contributes to the underuse of diagnostic and therapeutic epilepsy surgery,30 ultimately limiting quality of life improvement in all eligible patients. Historically, SDE was more common in the United States, but SEEG techniques have become dominant in the last decade.20 Current data comparing different iEEG modalities remain limited. In this study we identify one of the largest single-institution retrospective cohorts undergoing SEEG, SDE, or hybrid iEEG monitoring, and report on comparative surgical effectiveness and morbidity outcomes.

In lieu of randomized controlled trials, clinical standards are mostly derived from expert opinion,12,25,28,31 single-center retrospective studies with relatively small sample sizes and unbalanced cohort sizes,23,32,33 and meta-analyses, which often do not directly compare the modalities and are limited by heterogeneity between studies.28,29 In these studies, iEEG approaches are typically binarized into SDE and SEEG, where any SDE plus depth electrodes are grouped into SDE, thereby limiting nuanced analyses between modalities. As such, outcomes of hybrid iEEG are poorly characterized. Finally, neuromodulation is being increasingly used in the treatment of drug-resistant epilepsy,34 yet the role of iEEG in guiding neuromodulation and the impact on seizure response remain unclear.

### Surgical Yield

Traditionally, undertaking neurosurgical intervention after iEEG depended on satisfactory localization of the SOZ and an acceptable risk/benefit calculation with respect to resection of the putative SOZ.24 In our study, patients in the SDE cohort were more likely to undergo resection than those in the SEEG group, which is consistent with other studies and meta-analyses.14,24,28,35 However, we found that patients in the SEEG group were more likely to have their SOZ localized than were those who underwent pure SDE monitoring. Hence, beyond robust SOZ localization, additional factors are likely to contribute to this discrepancy.

One possible factor is the propensity for bias toward resection in cases with equivocal data after SDE monitoring, because a craniotomy has already been performed. Given that SDE explantation and resection can be carried out in the same operation, resective surgery may be more readily offered. Additionally, patient factors are an important source of bias, such that a patient who accepts the potential morbidity of SDE may be more inclined to undergo subsequent resection, even when iEEG localization is suboptimal or in a higher-risk zone. Finally, the regular spacing of SDE electrodes over the cortical surface may allow more precise functional mapping of eloquent cortex to facilitate resection in higher-risk SOZ locations.16 These trends are corroborated with the patients undergoing craniotomy in the hybrid cohort; they are also more likely to undergo subsequent resection than the SEEG group.

We also note that patients in the hybrid cohort were more likely to have their SOZ localized than were those in the SDE group. Given the coverage of both superficial and deep brain areas afforded by hybrid iEEG, it is possible that this approach increased the likelihood of detecting distinct SOZs or patterns of early spread, which would have been poorly localized with either SEEG or SDE alone. However, these additionally localized SOZs were probably thought to be not amenable to treatment, given that there were no differences with proceeding to subsequent treatment or resection.

Notably, we found no differences between SEEG and SDE groups with respect to undergoing any subsequent neurosurgical intervention, including neuromodulation. This suggests that in cases not amenable to the gold standard of resection, palliative methods such as RNS, DBS, and VNS are equally favored. Given that these are predominantly less invasive therapeutic modalities, the lack of association is reasonable because the risk and convenience considerations identified above for SDE/resection are moot. Recent evidence suggests that LITT is increasingly being offered as the first procedure, followed by resection if appropriate.36 Given that LITT is minimally invasive, it remains highly possible that SEEG might more likely be associated with LITT than is SDE or hybrid monitoring. However, because we evaluated only the first procedure and were limited by the sample size for LITT, we were not able to draw robust conclusions about its role.

### Seizure Outcomes

If resection is performed, postoperative seizure outcomes are largely a function of successful SOZ localization and complete resection of the epileptogenic foci. We found similar rates of favorable seizure outcomes in patients undergoing resection in the SEEG cohort and in the SDE cohort. Conflicting results have been reported in the literature thus far, with some studies corroborating our lack of difference in seizure outcomes,9,17,35,37 whereas other investigations suggest improved outcomes with SEEG.14,24,28 Discrepancies are likely to be due to differences in institutional practices and surgical candidate selection, cohort heterogeneity, and variability in seizure outcome assessments (in which some studies report on completely seizure-free outcomes, others on Engel class I outcomes, and others on favorable seizure outcomes). When compared to the cohort reported in Jehi et al.,24 our patients were more likely to have bilateral GTC seizures and to undergo bilateral iEEG investigations. This may suggest that our patient cohort at baseline might have had more complex seizure manifestations, which may contribute to the discrepancy in seizure outcomes.

Of note, we found no differences in seizure outcomes despite a higher likelihood of undergoing resection in the group with SDE, suggesting a better selection of candidates. The clinical value of iEEG is largely driven by the strength and clarity of the implantation hypothesis, technical feasibility of sampling relevant brain areas, and interpretation of ictal onset versus spread patterns.38 The emphasis on designing a comprehensive implantation strategy to define the epileptic network is particularly high in SEEG.24 Furthermore, the risk/reward balance probably favors more judicious patient selection for resection with SEEG, given that a craniotomy has yet to be performed.

Finally, in patients who underwent neuromodulation, there were no significant differences among favorable seizure outcomes across the modalities. A prior study evaluating these endpoints revealed similar results.14 These findings may suggest that the choice of iEEG investigation does not impact neuromodulation outcomes; however, the application of traditional epilepsy surgery metrics to neuromodulation therapy may fail to capture relevant patient-specific and quality of life outcomes. It is also very likely that the clinical decision-making for iEEG implantation strategy would take into account the possible or probable plan for subsequent neuromodulation.

### Surgical Complications

Compared to SDE and hybrid iEEG, we found that SEEG is associated with a lower risk of complications and infections, consistent with other studies.8,14,17,24,28,37,39,40 Furthermore, we noted trends of higher risk of SDHs with craniotomy procedures and a higher risk of IPHs with SEEG. However, the low incidence of these complications probably prevented statistical significance.

### Limitations

This large retrospective cohort adds to the growing literature comparing outcomes of SEEG and SDE, with additional characterization of hybrid iEEG investigations and neuromodulatory interventions. Nevertheless, our study is not exhaustive in evaluating all distinct scenarios where one technique may be superior to another. Many patient-specific clinical situations in which outcomes would not follow these overall trends may be masked in the comparison of SDE, SEEG, and hybrid iEEG in a pooled cohort analysis. Our statistical power declines when substratified; hence, lack of superiority with respect to some outcomes must be interpreted with caution. Similarly, we note a lack of standardization for the choice between procedures. We do note that in our cohort, SDE cases were completed earlier, whereas SEEG cases were completed later in the cohort. To address this confounder, we limited our analyses to 2015, where a similar number of cases of each iEEG type were carried out. We only noted a change with respect to SOZ localization, where there was no difference between patients in the SEEG and SDE cohorts. This suggests that time and technology have improved SOZ localization in patients who undergo SEEG monitoring; however, proceeding to any surgery or resection or having favorable seizure outcomes has not changed. Finally, we are limited by the single-center, retrospective nature of our data. Although mitigated by clinical decision-making and procedures performed independently at 2 sites by multiple neurosurgeons, it is impossible to eliminate all sources of selection and institution bias. Our study spanned nearly 2 decades; hence, practice variability over time was not robustly controlled for in these analyses.

## Conclusions

Our study presents a comprehensive analysis of one of the largest single-institution retrospective cohorts evaluating the outcomes of iEEG approaches. Patients monitored with SEEG were more likely to have their SOZ localized than were those who underwent SDE, but were less likely to undergo subsequent resection or to have complications. Patients in the SEEG and SDE cohorts were equally likely to undergo any neurosurgical treatment for epilepsy, including neuromodulation, and had similar seizure outcomes. Patients in the hybrid group were more likely to have their SOZ localized and to undergo subsequent treatment, including resection, but did not have superior seizure outcomes.

## Abstract

Large‐vessel occlusion (LVO) ischemic stroke is responsible for significant morbidity and mortality. We have previously described a novel tool for acute LVO detection that combines blood‐based biomarkers (glial fibrillary acidic protein and d‐dimer) with stroke severity scales to achieve high accuracy. Accordingly, the present study sought to prospectively validate cutoff values that we had previously established for biomarkers and scales.

The TIME (Testing for Identification Markers of Stroke) trial was designed as a prospective observational diagnostic accuracy study. All ambulance‐identified stroke code activations <18 hours from symptom onset were recruited at Brandon Regional Hospital (Brandon, FL) between May 2021 and August 2022. Previously determined cutoff concentrations of plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (213 pg/mL) and d‐dimer (600 ng/mL) were used in combination with prehospital stroke scales to detect LVO. We compared rates of LVO detection against a reference standard using computed tomography/magnetic resonance angiography.

A total of 382 patients with suspected stroke were recruited. The final cohort was composed of 323 patients with suspected stroke with the following distribution: LVO ischemic stroke (n = 29, 9%), non‐LVO ischemic stroke (n = 48, 15%), hemorrhagic stroke (n = 13, 4%), transient ischemic attack (n = 12, 3.9%), and stroke mimics (n = 220, 68.1%). Combining blood‐based biomarkers (glial fibrillary acidic protein and d‐dimer) with the scale field assessment stroke triage for emergency destination yielded the best performance for LVO detection, with specificity of 94% and sensitivity of 71%. Performance was found to be higher in a subanalysis focusing on patients presenting <6 hours from symptom onset, with 93% specificity and 81% sensitivity. Critically, application of the biomarker and stroke scale algorithms ruled out all patients with hemorrhage.

The present work prospectively validated the potential utility of previously defined glial fibrillary acidic protein and d‐dimer cutoff levels (ie, 213 pg/mL and 600 ng/mL, respectively), demonstrating their value for discrimination of LVO stroke from differential diagnoses during code stroke workups. ## Clinical Perspective

- The present study validates the effectiveness of using plasma biomarkers (GFAP [glial fibrillary acidic protein] and d‐dimer) in combination with stroke severity scales to detect large‐vessel occlusion ischemic strokes. High specificity (93/94%) and sensitivity (81/71%) was demonstrated at <6 and 18 hours.

- Implementation of these biomarkers in the pre‐hospital setting can aid in rapid and accurate triage of stroke patients.

- The biomarker algorithm effectively rules out hemorrhagic strokes, minimizing the risk of inappropriate treatment and facilitating targeted care.

The global disease burden of stroke is vast and continues to be a leading cause of human suffering. 1 , 2 , 3 A considerable proportion of this burden is driven by ischemic strokes caused by large‐vessel occlusions (LVOs). In fact, LVO accounts for 62% of poststroke disabilities and 96% of poststroke death. 4

Acute ischemic stroke with LVO is one of the most readily treatable stroke types, attributable to a recent paradigm shift toward endovascular thrombectomy (EVT). 5 Thrombectomy is effective but requires specialized teams and equipment, limiting its availability to comprehensive stroke centers and other EVT‐capable centers, which represent a small subset of accredited stroke centers and an even smaller subset of emergency medical facilities. 6 Transfers result in time delays, which in turn are associated with poor outcomes and significant increases in morbidity/death. 7 For every 15‐minute reduction from stroke onset to EVT treatment, there is a 3.9% decrease in long‐term disability; 2.5 times more patients also achieve functional independence (modified Rankin scale 0–2). 8 Delays in treatment often arise from interhospital transfer (ie, from primary stroke centers to EVT‐capable centers are estimated to delay treatment >2 hours) 8 or in the identification of candidate patients undergoing EVT with LVO strokes. 9 Therefore, early identification of patients with LVO in the prehospital setting (eg, within an ambulance) is critical to facilitating appropriate triage and routing patients to EVT‐capable centers in a timely manner. 10 Furthermore, early identification can expedite time to EVT and may facilitate direct transfer to the angiography suite. 11

A growing body of work has, therefore, evaluated prehospital stroke assessment scales in an effort to identify LVO strokes in the field. However, such severity scales lack the sensitivity and specificity required for triaging LVO patients with confidence, resulting in false negatives in patients with LVO as well as false positives in patients with stroke mimics or hemorrhagic stroke. 12 , 13 , 14 More accurate diagnostic tests complementing such clinical assessment scores are desperately needed. We have previously described a retrospective observational cohort study, demonstrating that combination of d‐dimer and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) with established stroke scales can accurately identify patients with LVO. 15

Herein, we describe the TIME (Testing of Identification Markers for Stroke) trial, which aims to prospectively assess the specificity and sensitivity of our predetermined biomarker/scale cutoff values for the identification of LVO versus non‐LVO stroke (ie, ischemic non‐LVO, hemorrhagic, stroke mimics, and transient ischemic attacks [TIAs]).

## Methods

### Study Design and Sample Collection

Data are available on reasonable request. We conducted an observational prospective cohort clinical trial wherein consecutive patients admitted by ambulance or the emergency department at the Brandon Regional Hospital in Florida between May 2021 and August 2022 were included if (1) they were referred for a suspected stroke and (2) the time from symptom onset was known to be <18 hours. The decision to include patients within 0 to 18 hours of symptom onset was based on the premise that the ability to detect LVO should lead to an actionable intervention, that is, leaving a window of time for advanced imaging, triage, and treatment (0–24 hours). Patients were excluded if they received thrombolytic therapy before collection of blood, if there was an anticipated inability to provide a blood sample, if the time from stroke onset was >18 hours, or if they were participating in a clinical trial related to an investigational medicinal product at the time of consent.

Collected venous whole blood was centrifuged at 4°C for 15 minutes at 10 000g and the obtained plasma was then frozen at −80°C until analysis. Frozen samples were transferred to Pockit Diagnostics Ltd for the assaying of biomarkers. WCG Western Institutional Review Board reviewed and approved this study (Institutional Review Board tracking number: 20193270; study number: 1294597).

### Clinical Data Collection

The following routine clinical data were collected for eligible patients: demographics (age, sex), clinical characteristics (blood pressure, pulse, atrial fibrillation, hypertension), clinical laboratory results (hematology, biochemistry, blood lipids), admission National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score by neurology‐trained clinicians, time since last known well, imaging findings within 1 hour, and final clinical diagnosis.

### Assigning a Diagnostic Category

The clinical data were used to assign patients to 1 of the following diagnostic categories: (1) LVO, (2) non‐LVO ischemic stroke, (3) hemorrhagic stroke, and (4) TIA/stroke mimic condition.

- LVO required computed tomography or magnetic resonance (MR) angiography confirmation of filling defect (ie, via a neuroradiology report) of: cervical or intracranial internal carotid artery, bifurcation of the internal carotid artery, cervical or intracranial vertebral artery, basilar artery, or first segment of middle cerebral artery (M1) before the major bifurcation/trifurcation or the insular turn, whichever occurred later, or second middle cerebral carotid artery segment (before the lateral insular turn) (M2), or the first or second segments of the anterior cerebral artery or posterior cerebral artery.

- Non‐LVO ischemic stroke required computed tomography or MR angiography exclusion via a neuroradiology report; that is, confirming the absence of LVO. In addition, diffusion restriction MR imaging was used to confirm ischemic stroke.

- Hemorrhagic stroke was assigned on the basis of the presence of hemorrhage on computed tomography (hyperdensity) or MR angiography (gradient echo or susceptibility weighted sequences or evident blood product on T1 or T2 sequences).

- TIA and stroke mimic(s) were assigned on the basis of expert clinical opinions and lack of pertinent findings on imaging.

The non‐LVO category used for determination of diagnostic performance was composed of TIAs, stroke mimics, hemorrhagic stroke, and non‐LVO ischemic stroke. The nonhemorrhagic suspected stroke subgroup used to compare GFAP levels versus hemorrhagic patients was composed of TIAs, stroke mimics, LVO ischemic stroke, and non‐LVO ischemic stroke.

### Derivation of Stroke Scales Fatrrom NIHSS Score

The same stroke scales used in our retrospective study were selected for consistency. 15 The face, arm, speech, time score was calculated by assigning 1 point for the presence of facial paresis (NIHSS item 4), 1 point for any arm weakness (NIHSS item 5a/b), and 1 point for any speech impairment (NIHSS item 9 or NIHSS item 10). Field assessment stroke triage for emergency destination (FAST‐ED) was calculated as described by Lima et al, 16 rapid arterial occlusion evaluation (RACE) score was calculated as described by Pérez de la Ossa, 17 Cincinnati stroke triage assessment tool was calculated as described by Katz et al, 18 and emergency medical stroke assessment was calculated as described by Gropen et al. 19

### Measurement of Blood Biomarkers

Plasma GFAP and d‐dimer were measured using commercially available enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assays following the manufacturer's instructions. d‐dimer enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assays kits (ab260076) and GFAP matched antibody pairs (ab222279) were purchased from Abcam (Cambridge, UK). All samples were analyzed in duplicate, and the mean value was used for quantification. For all patients, the coefficient of variation between replicates had to be <20%. All readings were performed with a CLARIO PLUS 430‐2070 ACU and Clariostar Plus Reader Control and MARS Software version 3.42 R5 (BMG Labtech, Cary, NC). Biomarker quantification was achieved via regression analysis of an 8‐point standard curve with known concentrations of analyte.

### Statistical Analysis

The intended use of the blood biomarkers was to rule in patients with LVO allowing for redirection of patients to EVT‐capable centers; accordingly, the study was powered for specificity. With a prevalence of 10% and a minimum specificity of 90%, a 2‐tailed 5% type I error rate (α) and 90% power (β), a sample size of 292 suspected patients with 29 LVOs would yield a specificity of 95% (95% CI, 90%–100%) for LVO. Ultimately, the final sample size was increased by ≈30% in an effort to account for possible data loss–related exclusion(s) criteria and the like.

To compare the levels of blood biomarkers and clinical variables in patients with and without LVO, the Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney U test, median, and interquartile range (IQR) were used. Categorical variables were dichotomized and assessed via a Pearson's χ2 test. Multiple hypothesis correction was performed using the Benjamini–Hochberg method.

Clinical decision rules combining previously identified cutoff values for d‐dimer, GFAP, and clinical scales were used to assign a “test‐positive” or “test‐negative” value. 15 , 20 In short, the cutoff used for plasma d‐dimer and GFAP were 600 ng/mL and 213 pg/mL, respectively. The cutoffs used for each prehospital clinical scale were as follows: Cincinnati stroke triage assessment tool >1, emergency medical stroke assessment >2, face, arm, speech, time >1, FAST‐ED >2, RACE >2. A “test‐positive” value was assigned on the basis of the following decision rule: clinical scale>cutoff+d‐dimer>600 ng/mL+GFAP<213 pg/mL.

To determine the diagnostic performance of each combination of biomarkers and clinical scale, confusion matrices were constructed using the LVO or non‐LVO diagnosis (see Assigning a Diagnostic Category section) and the assigned test‐positive or test‐negative values.

A subanalysis was conducted using only patients who presented within the first 6 hours since the time of last known well.

All analyses were performed with RStudio version 2023.03.0+386 (RStudio, PBC, Boston, MA). The data collected during the study are available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request.

## Results

### Study Enrollment

Of 382 patients recruited, 59 patients were excluded from further analyses (as outlined in Figure 1). Reasons for exclusion were absence of computed tomography/MR angiography data (n = 7), no NIHSS score documented at admission (n = 20), unknown time since last known well (n = 10), or absence of a blood sample (n = 22). The final cohort of 323 patients with suspected stroke was categorized as follows: LVO ischemic stroke (n = 29 [9%]), non‐LVO ischemic stroke (n = 48 [15%]), hemorrhagic stroke (n = 13 [4%]), TIA (n = 12 [3.7%]), and stroke mimics (n = 220 [68.1%]). Among the stroke mimic population, the diagnoses were as follows: encephalopathy (n = 26 [11.8%]), hyperglycemia (n = 2 [0.9%]), hypertensive emergency (n = 7 [3.2%]), migraine (n = 10 [4.5%]), posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (n = 1 [0.5%]), seizure (n = 17 [7.7%]), and undetermined (n = 157 [71.4%]). Among patients with LVO, 19 (66%) received EVT treatment. The following occlusions were observed in patients with LVO: A2 (n = 1 [3.4%]), internal carotid artery (n = 9 [31%]), middle cerebral artery M1 (n = 13 [44.9%]), middle cerebral carotid artery M2 (n = 5 [17.3%]), and posterior cerebral artery (n = 1 [3.4%]).

### Blood Biomarkers

The concentration of plasma d‐dimer was significantly higher in patients with LVO as compared with patients with non‐LVO suspected stroke (LVO suspected stroke, 1213 ng/mL [IQR, 733–1609] versus non‐LVO suspected stroke, 617 ng/mL [IQR, 377–1345]; P<0.001). GFAP was significantly increased in the plasma of patients with hemorrhagic stroke as compared with all other patients with suspected stroke (hemorrhagic stroke, 1464 pg/mL [IQR, 292–2580] versus nonhemorrhagic suspected stroke, 48 pg/mL [IQR, 12–98]; P<0.005).

### Diagnostic Performance for LVO Detection

Table 2 shows the diagnostic performance of the combination of plasma d‐dimer and GFAP with a number of different prehospital clinical symptom scales. Combinations of the blood biomarkers with the scales FAST‐ED or RACE showed the best performance for LVO detection, with a specificity of 94% (for either scale combination) and a sensitivity of 71% for both scales. A subanalysis considering only patients presenting within the first 6 hours from symptom onset showed improved sensitivity, with the combination of biomarkers and FAST‐ED resulting in a specificity of 93% and sensitivity of 81% (Table 2). Figure 2 shows the proportion of stroke subtypes selected as test positive by the combination of d‐dimer, GFAP, and FAST‐ED. Importantly, we found that no patients with hemorrhagic stroke were selected as test positive. ## Discussion

The TIME trial is the first study to validate blood biomarker cutoff values for LVO detection using a prospective cohort design. The TIME trial results demonstrate that a combination of d‐dimer and GFAP in conjunction with established clinical stroke scales, including FAST‐ED and RACE, is effective in the identification of patients with LVO stroke. Furthermore, these results validate our previously defined cutoff values for d‐dimer and GFAP of 600 ng/mL and 213 pg/mL, respectively. 15 These results may aid in the development of a point‐of‐care diagnostic test capable of guiding prehospital LVO stroke triage.

In a previous prospective observational study, Ramos‐Pachón et al in 2021 reported that d‐dimer was associated with LVO 21 ; using a d‐dimer cutoff point of 1664.15 ng/mL with an NIHSS score ≥10, LVOs were detected with a specificity of 93% and a sensitivity of 35%. 21 In our subsequent retrospective observational study, combining d‐dimer/GFAP with FAST‐ED resulted in a sensitivity of 82% and a specificity of 98%. 15 The results of the present study demonstrated a lower, albeit high, sensitivity (71%), and a high specificity (94%) for identification of LVO stroke using d‐dimer/GFAP combined with FAST‐ED. In addition to the use of different stroke severity scales, the improvement in sensitivity compared with the earlier work by Ramos‐Pachón is likely due to the use of a lower d‐dimer cutoff value (600 versus 1664 ng/mL). The addition of GFAP to d‐dimer and clinical scales likely contributed to maintaining high levels of specificity, by excluding patients with hemorrhagic stroke. This is in line with prior work demonstrating that GFAP levels are elevated in patients with hemorrhagic stroke as compared with ischemic stroke, stroke mimics and TIAs. 22 , 23 Therefore, the use of a lower d‐dimer cutoff with the addition of GFAP may provide a significant improvement over previous studies as demonstrated here. Of note, diagnostic specificity was prioritized over sensitivity in our earlier retrospective work to minimize the selection of patients without LVO who are unlikely to benefit from admission to an EVT‐capable hospital (ie, non‐LVO ischemic and stroke mimic/TIAs), or patients who should be stabilized as soon as possible (ie, hemorrhagic stroke).

In both the present prospective work and our previous retrospective study, patients with hemorrhagic stroke had significantly elevated levels of GFAP. 15 Given that clinical stroke scales in patients with hemorrhagic stroke frequently suggest LVO and that these patients are not candidates for EVT, a tool capable of ruling out hemorrhage and identifying only nonhemorrhagic ischemic LVO is essential. This dilemma was further highlighted in the RACECAT (Transfer to the Closest Local Stroke Center Versus Direct Transfer to Endovascular Stroke Center of Acute Stroke Patients With Suspected Large Vessel Occlusion in the Catalan Territory) trial, 24 and in a recent secondary analysis of its data (ie, the inappropriate triage of patients with intracerebral hemorrhage [ICH] led to worse outcomes). 25 Patients were randomized to either direct transport to an EVT or the closest local stroke center. No clinical benefit was demonstrated when using the RACE stroke scale to triage alone, 24 highlighting the need for effective blood biomarkers to identify nonhemorrhagic LVO stroke. 26 Accordingly, the RACECAT secondary analysis highlights the importance of accurately ruling out ICH from nonhemorrhagic LVO in the field. 25

Although not the focus of our present study, early identification of ICH may also be beneficial. The early positive results of the recent ENRICH (Early Minimally Invasive Removal of Intracerebral Hemorrhage) trial, emphasizes the importance of accurately identifying ICH. 27 Although prior randomized controlled trials have demonstrated limited clinical benefit of ICH clot evacuation, 28 , 29 the early ENRICH results suggest improved 180‐day modified Rankin scale scores and death in patients undergoing minimally invasive transsulcal parafascicular surgical ICH clot evacuation. 27 In addition, a recent comprehensive retrospective analysis of 5 centers in Germany between 2008 and 2021 demonstrated the benefit of surgical decompression in patients with larger stroke volumes. 30 Such evidence highlights the potential of our biomarker profile to rule in ICH in the setting of low d‐dimer/high GFAP, and prompt neurosurgical referral may also have therapeutic utility.

Compared with our previous study, a decreased sensitivity was observed. 15 This could be explained, at least in part, by inclusion of patients up to 18 hours from symptom onset. In a subgroup analysis of the current study, including only patients presenting within the first 6 hours of symptom onset increased the sensitivity considerably (71% versus 81% for the FAST‐ED combination), with no apparent change in specificity (94% versus 93%). This difference may also be due to blood biomarker kinetics or to resolving symptoms at later presentations. However, the performance observed in both time windows (0–18 and 0–6 hours) is well within the CIs defined in our previous study for both specificity (92%–100%) and sensitivity (57%–96%). 15

The clinical scales FAST‐ED and RACE have recently been prospectively validated. 31 , 32 FAST‐ED showed a specificity of 48% and sensitivity of 80%, while RACE demonstrated a specificity of 65% and a sensitivity of 71% for LVO. The present work definitively shows that a combination of GFAP and d‐dimer with either FAST‐ED or RACE yields improved performance compared with the clinical scales alone.

A high number (≈67%) of suspected strokes were categorized as stroke mimics, higher than the mimic rate reported in larger cohorts (≈30%). Merino et al 33 assessed predictors of acute stroke mimics in 8187 consecutive patients seen at the National Institutes of Health program over a 10‐year period; of note, female sex and arrival in a personal vehicle were predictors of stroke mimics. In our cohort, the relatively high percentage of female patients (≈60%) and patients presenting by private vehicle (≈31%) may in part explain our high mimic rate.

Given the likely reasonable cost versus imaging of the combined GFAP/d‐dimer biomarker profile, stroke triage systems could be rationalized in settings beyond high‐income countries. This is of particular importance as the majority of the current and predicted stroke burden is within low‐ and middle‐income countries. 1 , 34 The importance of cost‐effective stroke care resource allocation is, therefore, of considerable interest. Importantly, the recent 2023 Lancet Commission on “Pragmatic Solutions to Reduce the Global Burden of Stroke” specifically highlighted diagnostics/biomarkers as an important component in combating global stroke disease burden. 34

Several limitations should be noted in the present work. First, stroke scores were derived from NIHSS scores performed by emergency department clinicians and not directly collected by emergency medical services staff. This may be important for FAST‐ED and RACE, both known to be more complex compared with FAST or emergency medical stroke assessment. Additionally, NIHSS reporting bias may have arisen as clinicians conducting NIHSS scoring may have had access to additional data as compared with stroke scales that would be collected by emergency medical services staff. Second, we used frozen blood samples for biomarker measurements. Only sparse data are available on the stability of frozen d‐dimer and GFAP 35 , 36 ; we cannot exclude the possibility that some of our negative results could be due to protein degradation. Third, diagnostic adjudication by an independent vascular neurologist was not performed in this study. Although official medical records were used, we cannot exclude that an independent adjudicator would have interpreted imaging and clinical data differently. Fourth, by choosing biomarker cutoffs designed to yield highly specific results, a certain number of LVOs are missed. However, as such patients default into “standard‐of‐care” triaging pathways, such a decision is unlikely to represent much clinical risk. Finally, biomarker measurements were performed with laboratory immunoassays; as such, prospective validation with point‐of‐care assays in pertinent clinical settings will ultimately be required.

In conclusion, the prospective evidence presented herein further validates that the d‐dimer and GFAP cutoff levels of 600 ng/mL and 213 pg/mL, respectively, combined with stroke scales is capable of accurately identifying patients with nonhemorrhagic LVO stroke.

Abstract BACKGROUND CONTEXT: Currently, there is no universally accepted method for assessing radiological fusion shortly after anterior cervical discectomy. Five-year follow-up radiological Xrays demonstrating solid fusion or absence of fusion provided a gold standard for comparison with various assessment methods. PURPOSE: Establishing the most accurate diagnostic test for earlier bony fusion assessment by comparing different cut-off values for the difference in interspinous distance and the change in Cobb angle on dynamic radiological images against the established gold standard. DESIGN: Posthoc analysis from the NEtherlands Cervical Kinematics (NECK) trial (NTR1289). PATIENT SAMPLE: A total of 40 patients with 1 level herniated disc that underwent anterior discectomy between 2010 and 2014 returned for a 5-year follow-up X-ray. OUTCOME MEASURES: Radiological outcome was assessed quantitatively and qualitatively by fusion on radiographic images 5 years after surgery. METHODS: Radiological dynamic X-rays were reviewed for fusion at 5-year follow-up by a senior spine surgeon. At this timepoint, bony continuity was indisputable and served as gold standard. Cobb angles and interspinous distances on ﬂexion-extension images were measured independently by 2 investigators. Optimum agreement between the gold standard and the 2 methods was assessed, evaluating varying cut-off values, considering sensitivity, speciﬁcity, and area under the curve (AUC). RESULTS: Dynamic radiographic assessments revealed fusion in 29 out of 40 patients (mean age: 49 years § 8; 23 women). For Cobb angle (optimal cut-off: ≤3.0˚), the AUC was 0.86 with 100% sensitivity and 72.7% speciﬁcity. For interspinous distance (optimal cut-off: ≤1.5 mm), the AUC was 0.89 with 96.6% sensitivity and 81.8% speciﬁcity. The highest AUC (0.91) was observed for combined cut-off values (Cobb angle ≤3.0˚ and interspinous distance ≤2.0 mm), yielding 100% sensitivity and 81.8% speciﬁcity. CONCLUSION: The combination of cut-off values ≤3.0˚ difference for Cobb angle and ≤2.0 mm difference for interspinous distance on lateral ﬂexion-extension X-rays was assessed to be an accurate diagnostic criterion for fusion evaluation. Introduction

Cervical radicular syndrome (CRS) is a common problem usually caused by cervical disc herniation [1,2]. Anterior cervical discectomy is a common procedure in this setting, wherin the herniated intervertebral disc is removed via an anterior approach [3−5]; subsequently a device is inserted between the 2 vertebral bodies to uphold foraminal height, ideally inducing bony fusion [6,7].

The speed and extent to which the adjacent corpora fuse are deemed important factors in success recovery after anterior discectomy [8]. Information on the accuracy and reliability of diagnostic methods remains scarce [5,7−10], and a deﬁnite and universally accepted method to evaluate bony fusion has not yet been established. Although some studies consider surgical exploration to be a gold standard, this approach is not favorable nor realistic in clinical practice [9].

Existing work has shown a variety of assessment methods [7,9,11]. Fusion has commonly been deﬁned as the presence of trabecular bridging on lateral radiographs or CT scans and/or absence of motion on ﬂexion/extension radiographs. However, these methods are qualitive, based on an expert’s subjective opinion. Quantitative assessments of fusion on lateral ﬂexion/extension X-rays include 1) evaluating the change in Cobb angle on the operated level or 2) measuring the difference in distance between the ends of the spinous processes (interspinous distance method [ISD]). In contemporary practice, there is a lack of consensus on the appropriate cut-off values for those different measurement methods. Although assessing fusion promptly after surgery is clinically relevant, the method to assess solid fusion should be evaluated at an extended postintervention period, as the clear visibility of novel fusion on Xrays might be compromised during the initial postoperative stage, despite fusion already being accomplished [12].

Five years after surgery, fusion becomes unequivocally observable on X-rays, and expert opinion can be regarded as a reliable gold standard [10,13,14]. A previously published study on the evaluation of the outcomes in a variety of intervertebral devices (the NECK-trial) included a 5-year follow-up (FU) timepoint. Several patients were willing to undergo a lateral X-ray of the cervical spine [10]. As such, the difference in distance between spinous processes’ ends and change in Cobb angle could be measured on the ﬂexion/extension X-rays at 5-year FU and compared to the established gold standard. By estimating the positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), sensitivity, speciﬁcity, and the area under the curve (AUC) of the methods, the aims of the present study were to establish

optimal cut-off values for the assessment of bony fusion earlier postoperative.

Material and methods

A posthoc analysis was performed on data collected as part of the NEtherlands Cervical Kinematics (NECK) trial [10,15], a prospective, double-blinded multicenter randomized clinical trial in which patients with cervical radiculopathy due to a cervical disc herniation were randomly subjected to anterior cervical discectomy with arthroplasty (ACDA), anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) or anterior cervical discectomy without an intervertebral device (ACD) between November 2010 and October 2014. All patients underwent single-level surgery. The Central Medical Ethics Committee of the Leiden University Medical Center, the Medical Ethics Committee Noord-Holland, and the boards of directors of the involved hospitals granted approval for the trial (Dutch Trial Register Number: NTR1289). Written informed consent was obtained from all patients. A total of 109 patients were initially included in the NECK trial. Patients (aged 18−65 years old) with radicular signs and symptoms in 1 or both arms (pain, paresthesia or paresis in a speciﬁc nerve root distribution) for at least 8 weeks and for whom conservative therapy failed were eligible for inclusion. Patients with previous cervical surgery (either anterior or posterior), absence of motion, increased anteroposterior translation, very narrow (<3 mm) intervertebral space, severe segmental kyphosis (>3˚) at the index level on static or dynamic X-rays, neck pain only and symptoms and signs of myelopathy were excluded. Furthermore, patients with metabolic and bone diseases (osteoporosis, severe osteopenia), neoplasm or trauma of the cervical spine, spinal anomaly (Klippel Feil, Bechterew, OPLL), severe mental or psychiatric disorders were excluded [10]. Patients underwent either ACDA with an activC ﬂat artiﬁcial cervical disc, ACDF with an interbody PEEK cage ﬁlled with synthetic bone substitute or autologous bone (chips locally harvested), or ACD without an intervertebral device. A total of 56 patients returned for a 5- year FU image (Fig. 1). Out of these 56 patients, 15 were excluded due to missing of the ﬂexion-extension images. In 1 patient, the inferior endplate and spinous processes ends were not visible on the X-ray. Therefore, 40 patients were included in this study.

Notably, there is an overlap in patients with prior published works, which primarily focused on differences in clinical and radiological outcomes after ACDA, ACDF and ACD [10,15]. In contrast, our current study speciﬁcally

Qualitative assessment of fusion

All patients were assessed for fusion status in a random order on lateral X-rays by a senior spine surgeon with 18 years of experience, blinded to the clinical condition of the patients. Fusion was clearly visible as bone bridging of the gap between the vertebra on the

radiological images 5-years postoperative (Fig. 2). Therefore, expert opinion at 5-years FU was considered as the gold standard.

Quantitative assessment of fusion

Two investigators independently performed these measurements, both using the same measurement program (PACS Sectra IDS7). The 2 investigators were trained to perform these measurements by a senior spine surgeon.

Both investigators were blinded to the other investigator’s measurements.

To determine whether the ﬂexion and extension performed by the patient was adequate, the Cobb C2-C7 cervical angle of all patients was measured. To that end the angle between the line drawn parallel to the caudal endplate of C2 and the line drawn parallel to the caudal endplate of C7 was measured in ﬂexion and extension and the difference was taken as the ﬂexion extension C2-7 angle.

To determine the fusion at the target level, 2 measurements were performed on ﬂexion and extension X-rays (Fig. 3): 1) the Cobb angles of the operated level were measured as the angle between the line drawn parallel to the rostral endplate of the upper vertebral body and the line drawn parallel to the caudal endplate of the lower vertebral body. The difference between the angle in ﬂexion and the angle in extension was calculated; 2) the distances between the distal ends of the spinous processes adjacent to the operated level were measured. The difference between the distance in ﬂexion and in extension was calculated.

Cut-off values

Quantitative determination of fusion by assessing the difference between 2 measurements will contain some margin or error. Various values for this margin of error were described in the literature [11,16−22]. By comparing these measurements against the gold standard at 5-year FU (expert opinion), sensitivity and speciﬁcity could be calculated. For the Cobb angle method, sensitivity, speciﬁcity, PPV, NPV and AUC were calculated with an accepted margin of error of ≤2˚, 2.5˚, and 3˚, separately. For the ISD methods, sensitivity, speciﬁcity, PPV, NPV and AUC were

calculated with an accepted margin of error of ≤1, 1.5, and 2 mm, separately. The area under the curve (AUC) is the percent chance that the model will be able to classify an outcome correctly, in this study fusion versus no fusion. The closer the AUC is to 1, the better the model is with the chosen cut-off values at distinguishing between fusion and no fusion. Additionally, different combinations of cut-off values for the 2 measurement were evaluated.

Statistics

Demographic data are presented either as the mean (with standard deviation [SD]) or an absolute number.

For the difference in ISD and the difference in Cobb angle on the ﬂexion-extension images, interobserver variance was calculated using the Intraclass Correlation Coefﬁ- cient (ICC) (0−0.20 [slight agreement], 0.21−0.40 [fair agreement], 0.41−0.60 [moderate], 0.61−0.80 [substantial agreement], 0.81−1.00 [almost perfect agreement]) [23]. Furthermore, the sensitivity, speciﬁcity, PPV and NPV, and AUC were calculated for the different cut-off values and for multiple combinations of the cut-off values for the 2 measurement methods.

All statistics were performed using IBM SPSS software, version 28.0.

Reports on fusion rates after anterior cervical spine surgery vary, with mean fusion rates ranging from 30% to 100%, as assessed by a systematic review from 2019 [7]. This substantial variance can be explained by a variety in (short) FU periods and mainly qualitative evaluation methods. Prior systematic reviews evaluating fusion assessment methods have concluded that an optimal method could not be determined, as a gold standard has been missing [7,8].

The 5-year evaluation of the radiological images from the NECK trial supplied us with X-rays that undeniably demonstrated bone bridging of the gap between the vertebra created during surgery, and thus provided a gold standard. It is remarkable that 11 out of 40 patients did not demonstrate solid fusion 5 years after surgery. The values retrieved in assessing the differences in Cobb angles and interspinous distances corresponded well to the evaluation of the expert, adding to the validity of the expert opinion.

The vast majority of available articles on fusion evaluation used X-rays or CT scans conducted shortly postoperatively. Ideally, fusion should be evaluated longitudinally, considering various time points. During the evaluation period of the NECK trial, additional X-rays were taken at 1- and 2-year FU. The presence of the bone bridging between the 2 vertebrae, however, was not yet evident at those intervals. It is plausible that clinically relevant fusion was accomplished at those earlier timepoints, but this could not yet be objectively conﬁrmed as it was not yet clearly visible on the images. This underscores the need for a quantitative measurement method to assess fusion during these

timepoints, as it is clinically relevant to establish (the absence of) fusion earlier on.

A previous attempt to assess the diagnostic accuracy of radiographic fusion conducted by Riew et al, employed surgical exploration of the alleged fused cervical vertebrae as the gold standard [11]. Intraoperative evidence of fusion was compared with 1 quantitative measurement on X-ray (interspinous distance <1 mm and super adjacent spinous motion >4 mm) and 3 qualitative assessments of bone bridging on CT scan. The sole quantitative method among those criteria, the difference in interspinous distance <1 mm, showed a sensitivity of 70.1% and a speciﬁcity of 91.4%.

Cannada et al [24] reported quantitative measurements to assess fusion and compared the accuracy of the change in Cobb angle and the difference in distance between the tips of the spinous processes at the operated levels in diagnosing pseudoarthrosis. The only cut-off values they reviewed were a Cobb angle of 2˚ showing a ROC of 0.66 and interspinous distance of 2 mm, showing a ROC curve of 0.98. However, no gold standard was available as comparison method.

There were a few limitations to this study. First, our sample size was relatively small, which possibly increased standard deviation and increased the impact of small measurement errors. Furthermore, we evaluated adequacy of the ability of the patient to ﬂex and deﬂex the cervical column by evaluation of the C2−C7 angle. Currently, there is no gold standard to deﬁne this. The measure is consistent though with the C2−C7 angle presented in a previous study on the range of motion in the cervical spine (37.9˚+/11.2˚)

Given the differences in technique and ultimate objectives among these operations, it is conceivable that these groups may not be entirely comparable. However, because we are not assessing clinical outcomes of the surgery but solely conducting measurements on the images for fusion assessment, this should not have impacted the results.

Conclusion

Combining the cut-off values ≤3.0˚ difference for Cobb angle and ≤2.0 mm difference for interspinous distance on lateral ﬂexion-extension X-rays could be recommended as diagnostic criteria to establish fusion postoperatively. To validate these cut-off values, further research is required, including a larger sample size with only patients who have undergone anterior cervical discectomy and fusion.

## Abstract

Glioblastoma is the most common and lethal central nervous system malignancy with a median survival after progression of only 6–9 months. Major biochemical mechanisms implicated in glioblastoma recurrence include aberrant molecular pathways, a recurrence-inducing tumor microenvironment, and epigenetic modifications. Contemporary standard-of-care (surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, and tumor treating fields) helps to control the primary tumor but rarely prevents relapse. Cytoreductive treatment such as surgery has shown benefits in recurrent glioblastoma; however, its use remains controversial. Several innovative treatments are emerging for recurrent glioblastoma, including checkpoint inhibitors, chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy, oncolytic virotherapy, nanoparticle delivery, laser interstitial thermal therapy, and photodynamic therapy. This review seeks to provide readers with an overview of (1) recent discoveries in the molecular basis of recurrence; (2) the role of surgery in treating recurrence; and (3) novel treatment paradigms emerging for recurrent glioblastoma.

Keywords: recurrent glioblastoma, neurosurgery, neuro-oncology

## 1. Introduction

Glioblastoma is the most common and aggressive primary central nervous system (CNS) tumor. The current standard of care for newly diagnosed glioblastoma includes maximal safe resection followed by radiation therapy and temozolomide (TMZ) [1]. Moreover, regimens adding tumor treating fields (TTFs) are increasingly being considered standard of care [2]. Other variations in treatment protocols include differences depending on age and methylation status of O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) [3,4,5]. However, despite well-established protocols for initial treatment and continued efforts to improve treatment options, the median overall survival for newly diagnosed glioblastoma remains poor at 15.6 months after initial treatment, with recurrence typically occurring within 6–9 months of initial diagnosis [6,7].

Maximal safe resection represents the cornerstone of current newly diagnosed glioblastoma treatment, demonstrating both a survival benefit and improved quality of life [8]. As such, new techniques have been developed to maximize resections such as intraoperative MRI or fluorescent guiding agents like 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA), which preferentially accumulates in malignant tissues as protoporphyrin IX [9,10,11,12,13]. However, the complete removal of tumor cells is not possible with contemporary surgery as infiltrating glioblastoma cells persist in the brain, extending beyond the visible tumor [14,15,16]. In fact, postmortem studies have demonstrated that neoplastic cells extend beyond visible enhancement on imaging, making even supramaximal surgery non-curative [17]. Furthermore, as a consequence of initial chemoradiotherapy, residual tumor cells may undergo epigenetic modifications and acquire DNA mismatch repair mutations, which can induce resistance to subsequent therapy [18]. The resistance to chemotherapy and radiation and challenges concerning maximal safe resection continue to be core problems in treating recurrent glioblastoma.

Accordingly, this review first aims to summarize current research in recurrent glioblastoma such as the molecular pathways and genetic mutations that drive cell proliferation (TERT, PTEN, PI3K/Akt, MSH6, and LTBP4) and paracrine signaling of glioma stem cells (GSCs) [19,20]. Secondly, we discuss the advantages and limitations of resection in recurrent glioblastoma and alternatives including laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT). Finally, we discuss novel treatment paradigms in recurrent glioblastoma including checkpoint inhibitors, chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T cell) therapy, and OV therapy.

## 2. Molecular Mechanisms of Recurrence

### 2.1. Genetic Mutations in Newly Diagnosed Glioblastoma and Recurrent Glioblastoma

To understand the genetic and molecular mechanisms of recurrent glioblastoma, the changes from newly diagnosed glioblastoma to recurrent glioblastoma must be considered. Although the total number of genetic mutations is reported to be relatively stable between newly diagnosed and recurrent glioblastoma [16,21], several dominant mutations at initial diagnosis differ compared with recurrence (Table 1). In recurrent glioblastoma, there is the preservation of clonal mutations such as telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) [22] and phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) [23], with a relative loss of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations and amplification [21,24,25] and overexpression of platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGF-R). On the other hand, acquired hypermethylation of mismatch repair genes MSH6, LTBP4, and ALKBH5 are almost exclusively observed in recurrent glioblastoma post-initial treatment [21,26].
